A licence renewal is missed.
A policy becomes outdated.
A contract is signed without the right approval.
A tax obligation is misunderstood.
An employee process is handled inconsistently.
A regulatory change is not identified in time.

For a growing UAE business, these seemingly small gaps can develop into financial, operational, legal and reputational risks.

The UAE business environment includes requirements relating to areas such as taxation, licensing, employment, AML, data protection and sector-specific regulation. The exact obligations depend on the company's activities, legal structure and jurisdiction.

The real challenge for management is therefore not simply knowing that compliance matters.

It is knowing where the business is most exposed and whether the right controls are actually in place.

1. Licensing and Regulatory Requirements

One of the most basic—and potentially most disruptive—compliance risks is failing to maintain the licences, registrations or approvals required for the business.

This can happen when:

  • A licence expires.
  • The business changes its activities without reviewing licensing requirements.
  • A new service requires additional approval.
  • The company expands into a new jurisdiction.
  • Corporate information is not updated.

The risk increases as businesses grow and their activities become more complex.

Warning sign: Nobody has clear responsibility for monitoring licence and registration requirements.

2. VAT and Corporate Tax Compliance

Tax compliance is an important part of the UAE compliance landscape. The UAE applies VAT and corporate tax, with corporate tax applying to relevant businesses under the federal corporate tax framework.

Common risk areas can include:

  • Incorrect tax treatment
  • Missed filing deadlines
  • Inadequate records
  • Incorrect calculations
  • Weak supporting documentation
  • Failure to assess the tax implications of transactions
  • Inadequate review of related-party arrangements

Tax compliance should not be viewed as simply "filing the return."

The underlying accounting, documentation and controls matter as well.

Warning sign: Tax compliance depends entirely on an external accountant without sufficient internal management review.

3. Employment and HR Compliance

As the workforce grows, employment compliance becomes more difficult to manage informally.

Potential risk areas include:

  • Employment contracts
  • Employee records
  • Working arrangements
  • Leave and entitlements
  • Payroll
  • Disciplinary procedures
  • Termination processes
  • Workplace policies
  • Employee documentation

The UAE Government provides specific requirements covering private-sector employment, contracts, working arrangements and employee rights.

Warning sign: Different employees are treated differently because there are no clear HR policies or procedures.

4. AML and Customer Due Diligence

Certain UAE businesses have specific obligations relating to anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing.

Depending on the business and its activities, compliance may involve:

  • Customer identification
  • Customer due diligence
  • Risk assessment
  • Record keeping
  • Monitoring
  • Suspicious transaction reporting
  • Staff awareness and training

AML obligations are particularly important for businesses operating within relevant regulated sectors and designated non-financial activities.

Warning sign: The company accepts customers without a consistent process for assessing customer risk.

5. Data Protection and Privacy

Businesses increasingly hold significant amounts of personal and commercially sensitive information.

This may include:

  • Customer information
  • Employee data
  • Identification documents
  • Contact details
  • Financial information
  • Commercial information

Data protection obligations can vary depending on the applicable legal framework and jurisdiction. Certain UAE financial centres, for example, have their own data protection regimes.

Potential risks include:

  • Unauthorised access
  • Inappropriate data sharing
  • Poor retention practices
  • Inadequate security
  • Lack of clear privacy procedures

Warning sign: Employees can access customer or employee information without clearly defined access controls.

6. Contract and Commercial Compliance

Contracts can create significant compliance and commercial risks when they are not properly reviewed or managed.

Common issues include:

  • Unclear obligations
  • Missing approval processes
  • Unfavourable termination provisions
  • Inadequate liability protection
  • Poor confidentiality provisions
  • Unclear payment terms
  • Unmanaged renewal dates
  • Failure to meet contractual obligations

A company may technically be compliant with regulations but still suffer significant losses because it has poor contractual controls.

Warning sign: Employees are signing contracts without a defined approval or review process.

7. Corporate Governance Gaps

Compliance and corporate governance are different, but they are closely connected.

Governance weaknesses can include:

  • Unclear decision-making authority
  • Founder dependency
  • Poor board oversight
  • Weak management reporting
  • Undefined responsibilities
  • Inadequate conflict-of-interest procedures
  • Lack of shareholder clarity

These issues may not immediately result in a regulatory breach.

However, they can increase the company's overall risk exposure and become particularly important during investment, due diligence or expansion.

Warning sign: Major decisions are made informally without clear authority or documentation.

8. Weak Internal Controls

Internal controls are the mechanisms that help prevent errors, fraud, unauthorised transactions and other business risks.

Examples include controls over:

  • Payments
  • Bank accounts
  • Procurement
  • Expenses
  • Discounts
  • Payroll
  • Inventory
  • Customer credit
  • Capital expenditure

A growing company may continue using controls designed for a much smaller business.

That can create significant exposure.

Warning sign: The same individual can initiate, approve and execute a financial transaction without independent review.

9. Poor Record Keeping

Compliance is difficult to demonstrate if the company cannot produce evidence.

Potentially important records can include:

  • Corporate documents
  • Tax records
  • Contracts
  • Employee records
  • Approvals
  • Policies
  • Compliance reviews
  • Training records
  • Board minutes
  • Risk assessments

Poor record keeping can create problems during:

  • Regulatory reviews
  • Tax assessments
  • Legal disputes
  • Investor due diligence
  • M&A transactions

Warning sign: Management repeatedly has to search through emails and personal files to find important company documents.

10. Lack of Regulatory Monitoring

Compliance is not static.

Businesses need to consider whether changes in:

  • Regulations
  • Business activities
  • Products
  • Markets
  • Customers
  • Technology

create new compliance requirements.

The UAE Government's business platform covers a broad range of areas including business regulations, AML, intellectual property, taxation and insolvency.

Warning sign: The company only becomes aware of regulatory changes after an adviser, customer or regulator raises the issue.

11. Third-Party and Supplier Risk

Your business can also be exposed through third parties.

Suppliers, agents, consultants and outsourced service providers may have access to:

  • Company funds
  • Customer information
  • Personal data
  • Confidential information
  • Technology systems
  • Critical operations

Potential weaknesses include:

  • Limited due diligence
  • Weak contractual protections
  • No ongoing monitoring
  • Unclear responsibilities
  • Excessive system access

Warning sign: The company works with third parties based primarily on trust without documented risk assessment or contractual protections.

12. Conflicts of Interest

Conflicts can arise when directors, shareholders, employees or related parties have interests outside the company.

Examples could include:

  • A shareholder owning a supplier
  • A director having an interest in a competing business
  • A related party providing services to the company
  • An employee having a financial interest in a supplier

A conflict does not necessarily mean misconduct.

The risk arises when conflicts are not identified, disclosed and appropriately managed.

Warning sign: The company has no formal process for declaring and managing conflicts of interest.

13. Inadequate Policies and Procedures

A company may have policies simply because someone told management that it "needs policies."

The real question is:

Do employees actually use them?

Policies should address relevant business risks and should be supported by practical procedures.

Outdated or generic policies can create a false sense of security.

Warning sign: Policies have not been reviewed for several years or employees are unaware that they exist.

14. Lack of Compliance Training

Even a well-designed compliance framework can fail if employees do not understand it.

Employees should know:

  • What the company expects
  • What they are responsible for
  • What they must not do
  • When approval is required
  • When to escalate an issue

Training should be proportionate to the employee's role and the risks involved.

Warning sign: Employees regularly ask basic compliance questions because there is no structured awareness or training programme.

15. Founder Dependency

Founder-led businesses can be highly effective.

But when all compliance knowledge sits with the founder, the business becomes vulnerable.

Ask:

What happens if the founder is unavailable?

Who knows:

  • Which licences are required?
  • Which filings are due?
  • Which contracts are critical?
  • Which policies apply?
  • Which regulators are relevant?

A professionally managed company should gradually move from individual knowledge to institutional knowledge.

16. Compliance Gaps During Expansion

Growth creates new risks.

When a company:

  • Opens a new branch
  • Enters another emirate
  • Establishes a new entity
  • Expands internationally
  • Launches a new product
  • Enters a regulated market

it should reassess its compliance obligations.

The compliance framework that worked previously may no longer be sufficient.

Warning sign: Business expansion is planned commercially, but compliance implications are considered only after launch.

17. Compliance Risks During Investment or M&A

Investors and buyers may conduct extensive due diligence.

They may examine:

  • Corporate records
  • Licences
  • Tax
  • Employment
  • Contracts
  • Litigation
  • Regulatory matters
  • Policies
  • Internal controls

A compliance issue discovered during due diligence can create additional questions and potentially affect transaction negotiations.

For businesses considering investment or a sale, compliance readiness should ideally begin before the transaction process starts.

18. No Formal Compliance Ownership

Perhaps the most common risk is the simplest:

Nobody owns compliance.

Management assumes:

  • Finance handles it.
  • HR handles it.
  • Legal handles it.
  • The accountant handles it.
  • The founder handles it.

The result can be fragmented responsibility.

A practical compliance framework should establish:

What needs to be done → Who owns it → Who reviews it → When it is due → How it is evidenced.

A Practical Compliance Risk Checklist

Management should ask:

QuestionYes / No
Are all required licences and registrations monitored?
Are tax obligations properly managed?
Are employment processes documented?
Are applicable AML requirements addressed?
Is personal data appropriately managed?
Are contracts subject to appropriate review?
Are decision-making authorities clear?
Are internal financial controls effective?
Are important records properly maintained?
Are regulatory changes monitored?
Are key third parties assessed?
Are conflicts of interest managed?
Are policies reviewed regularly?
Do employees receive appropriate training?
Is compliance ownership clearly assigned?

A "No" does not automatically mean the company is non-compliant.

It indicates an area that may warrant further review.

The Biggest Compliance Risk Is Not Knowing Your Biggest Risk

Growing businesses rarely have unlimited resources.

The objective is therefore not to build an unnecessarily complicated compliance structure.

It is to identify the material risks, prioritise them and establish appropriate controls.

A practical approach is:

Identify → Assess → Prioritise → Control → Monitor → Report → Improve

This allows compliance to become part of normal business management rather than a reaction to problems.

How SHAAS Helps UAE Businesses Manage Compliance Risk

At SHAAS, we help businesses identify compliance gaps and build practical frameworks appropriate to their size, activities and growth objectives.

Our support can include:

  • Compliance health checks
  • Regulatory obligations mapping
  • Compliance risk assessments
  • Compliance frameworks
  • Policies and procedures
  • Internal controls
  • Compliance registers
  • Risk monitoring
  • Management reporting
  • Regulatory change management
  • Compliance remediation
  • Ongoing advisory support

We help management move from reactive compliance to structured compliance risk management.

Compliance Should Be Managed Before It Becomes a Problem

Compliance risks rarely improve simply because a business gets bigger.

In many cases, they become more complex.

The businesses that manage compliance effectively are not necessarily those with the largest compliance departments.

They are the businesses that understand:

What applies to them.

Where the risks are.

Who is responsible.

What controls are required.

How management knows those controls are working.

For UAE SMEs and growing companies, building this visibility early can help protect the business and provide a stronger foundation for sustainable growth.

title: Preparing Your Business for Regulatory Reviews and Due Diligence
excerpt: The worst time to discover that your business is not compliance-ready is when someone is already asking for the documents.
body:
The worst time to discover that your business is not compliance-ready is when someone is already asking for the documents.

A regulatory review, investor due diligence exercise, acquisition process or major client onboarding can quickly expose weaknesses that management may not have noticed during day-to-day operations.

Missing documents.
Expired licences.
Inconsistent contracts.
Unclear ownership.
Incomplete employee records.
Unresolved compliance issues.

Individually, these may appear manageable.

Together, they can create delays, additional scrutiny, unexpected costs and uncertainty about the quality of the business.

For UAE businesses, being prepared means more than having documents available. It means being able to demonstrate that the company has appropriate systems, controls, records and accountability in place.

What Is Regulatory Readiness?

Regulatory readiness means having the documentation, processes, controls and internal responsibilities necessary to respond effectively when a regulator or other authorised body reviews the business.

It involves being able to demonstrate:

  • What obligations apply to the company
  • How those obligations are managed
  • Who is responsible
  • What controls are in place
  • How compliance is monitored
  • What records support compliance
  • How issues are identified and resolved

The objective is not to prepare for a review by creating documents at the last minute.

The objective is to operate as though the business could be reviewed at any time.

Regulatory Review vs Due Diligence

These processes are not the same.

Regulatory Review

A regulator or competent authority may assess whether the company is complying with applicable laws, regulations, licensing conditions or regulatory requirements.

Due Diligence

An investor, buyer, lender or strategic partner may examine the company before entering into a transaction or relationship.

Due diligence can cover:

  • Legal
  • Financial
  • Tax
  • Commercial
  • Operational
  • HR
  • Regulatory
  • Governance

Both can reveal compliance weaknesses.

The difference is that regulatory reviews focus on compliance with applicable requirements, while due diligence evaluates the broader risk and quality of the business.

Why Businesses Get Caught Unprepared

Many companies operate successfully for years without formally reviewing their compliance position.

Management may assume:

"If there was a serious problem, we would know about it."

That assumption can be dangerous.

Compliance weaknesses are often invisible until someone asks specific questions.

For example:

Who is responsible for this obligation?

Where is the supporting documentation?

When was the last review performed?

What happens if this control fails?

Can you demonstrate that employees followed the procedure?

If management cannot answer these questions quickly, the company may not be as prepared as it believes.

1. Start With a Compliance Health Check

Before a regulatory review or due diligence process, management should assess the current position.

Review:

  • Licences
  • Registrations
  • Corporate records
  • Tax compliance
  • Employment records
  • Material contracts
  • Regulatory obligations
  • Policies
  • Internal controls
  • Data protection
  • AML requirements where applicable
  • Litigation and disputes

The objective is to identify gaps before an external party identifies them.

2. Verify Corporate and Licensing Records

Corporate records should be complete, current and consistent.

Depending on the company, this may include:

  • Trade licence
  • Constitutional documents
  • Shareholder information
  • Beneficial ownership information where applicable
  • Director and manager information
  • Regulatory registrations
  • Permits and approvals

Check that information is consistent across relevant documents and systems.

A discrepancy that seems minor internally may generate questions during due diligence.

3. Review Tax Compliance

Tax documentation should be organised and readily accessible.

Depending on the business, this may include:

  • VAT registration
  • VAT returns
  • Corporate Tax registration
  • Corporate Tax returns where applicable
  • Tax payment records
  • Supporting schedules
  • Tax correspondence
  • Relevant accounting records

The objective is not simply to show that filings were submitted.

Management should be able to explain how the underlying figures were determined and supported.

4. Review Material Contracts

Material commercial contracts are frequently examined during due diligence.

Review:

  • Customer contracts
  • Supplier agreements
  • Distribution agreements
  • Employment agreements
  • Partnership agreements
  • Financing arrangements
  • Lease agreements
  • Intellectual property agreements

Pay particular attention to:

  • Termination rights
  • Renewal dates
  • Change-of-control provisions
  • Exclusivity
  • Liability
  • Indemnities
  • Guarantees
  • Payment obligations
  • Dispute resolution
  • Unusual commitments

A business may have strong revenue but still face significant contractual risk.

5. Check Employment Documentation

HR documentation should be organised and consistent.

Depending on the business, this may include:

  • Employment contracts
  • Employee records
  • Policies
  • Payroll records
  • Leave records
  • Disciplinary documentation
  • Termination records
  • Confidentiality and IP arrangements

Inconsistencies between employees can create questions during a review or transaction.

6. Review Policies and Procedures

Policies should be:

Relevant.

Current.

Approved.

Communicated.

Implemented.

Common areas may include:

  • Code of Conduct
  • Anti-bribery
  • AML
  • Data protection
  • Information security
  • Conflict of interest
  • Whistleblowing
  • Procurement
  • Delegation of authority
  • HR procedures

A company having a policy is not enough.

If asked:

"How is this policy implemented?"

management should be able to provide a credible answer.

7. Test Internal Controls

Review whether key controls actually operate.

Consider:

  • Who can approve payments?
  • Who has access to bank accounts?
  • Who can sign contracts?
  • Who can approve discounts?
  • Who can hire employees?
  • Who can access sensitive data?
  • Are responsibilities appropriately segregated?

The objective is to identify control weaknesses before an external reviewer does.

8. Organise a Compliance Register

A compliance register can provide management with a consolidated view of:

  • Requirement
  • Responsible person
  • Frequency
  • Deadline
  • Evidence
  • Status
  • Outstanding actions

This can be particularly valuable during due diligence because management can quickly demonstrate that compliance is actively managed.

9. Resolve Known Issues

One of the most important preparation steps is to identify unresolved compliance matters.

Create an action register covering:

IssueRiskOwnerAction RequiredDeadlineStatus
Missing documentMediumFinanceObtain documentDateOpen
Policy outdatedLowHRReview policyDateOpen
Contract issueHighLegalReview agreementDateOpen

Not every issue needs to be fixed immediately.

The important thing is that management understands:

What is wrong?

How significant is it?

What is being done about it?

10. Prepare a Due Diligence Data Room

Businesses preparing for investment, acquisition or major transactions should consider establishing a structured data room.

Typical categories can include:

Corporate

  • Constitutional documents
  • Licences
  • Shareholder information

Financial

  • Financial statements
  • Management accounts
  • Tax records
  • Bank information

Legal

  • Material contracts
  • Litigation
  • Disputes
  • IP

HR

  • Employee information
  • Employment agreements
  • Policies

Regulatory

  • Licences
  • Regulatory correspondence
  • Compliance policies
  • Compliance reports

Commercial

  • Major customers
  • Major suppliers
  • Strategic agreements

The precise requirements will depend on the transaction.

11. Make Sure Information Is Consistent

One of the biggest due diligence warning signs is inconsistency.

For example:

  • Different shareholder information appears in different documents.
  • Revenue figures do not reconcile.
  • Contract values differ from accounting records.
  • Employee numbers differ between reports.
  • Corporate documents contain outdated information.

Inconsistencies create questions.

Questions create additional requests.

Additional requests create delays.

Accuracy and consistency are therefore critical.

12. Prepare Management to Answer Questions

Documentation is only one part of readiness.

Management may also be asked:

  • What are the company's major regulatory risks?
  • Who manages compliance?
  • How are policies approved?
  • How are risks monitored?
  • Have there been regulatory breaches?
  • Are there ongoing disputes?
  • How are related-party transactions managed?
  • What happens when a compliance issue is identified?

Management should provide clear, accurate and consistent answers.

Do not attempt to hide or minimise material issues.

Where a problem exists, it is generally better to explain:

What happened → What was the impact → What was done → How recurrence is being prevented.

13. Review Related-Party Transactions

Related-party arrangements can receive particular attention during due diligence.

Review transactions involving:

  • Shareholders
  • Directors
  • Founders
  • Related companies
  • Family members where relevant
  • Connected businesses

Check whether:

  • The relationship is properly disclosed.
  • Appropriate approvals were obtained.
  • Terms are documented.
  • Transactions are properly recorded.

This is particularly relevant for family-owned and founder-led businesses.

14. Review Regulatory Correspondence

Maintain an organised record of communications with relevant authorities.

This may include:

  • Regulatory notices
  • Requests for information
  • Responses
  • Approvals
  • Inspections
  • Findings
  • Remediation correspondence

If an issue was identified previously, maintain evidence showing how it was addressed.

15. Do Not Create Documents Just for the Review

A common mistake is attempting to "build compliance" immediately before an external review.

Creating policies overnight does not necessarily demonstrate an effective compliance culture.

A reviewer may reasonably ask:

When was this policy introduced?

Who approved it?

Were employees trained?

Has it been implemented?

Has compliance been monitored?

This is why compliance readiness should be treated as an ongoing management discipline, not a last-minute exercise.

16. Prepare for Investor Due Diligence

If your business may seek investment, preparation should begin well before investors arrive.

Investors may examine:

  • Corporate structure
  • Financial performance
  • Tax
  • Contracts
  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Employees
  • Intellectual property
  • Litigation
  • Regulatory matters
  • Governance
  • Internal controls

A business that is well organised can respond more quickly and confidently.

This can help create a perception of professionalism, transparency and management control.

17. Prepare for M&A

For companies considering an acquisition or sale, compliance readiness can become particularly important.

Potential buyers may identify issues that affect:

  • Valuation
  • Transaction structure
  • Warranties
  • Indemnities
  • Conditions precedent
  • Completion timelines

Addressing known issues before the transaction can reduce surprises during negotiations.

A Practical Regulatory & Due Diligence Readiness Checklist

Before a review or due diligence exercise, management should ask:

AreaReady?
Corporate documents✓ / ✗
Licences and registrations✓ / ✗
Beneficial ownership information✓ / ✗
Tax records✓ / ✗
Material contracts✓ / ✗
Employment records✓ / ✗
Policies and procedures✓ / ✗
Compliance register✓ / ✗
Internal controls✓ / ✗
Regulatory correspondence✓ / ✗
Litigation and disputes✓ / ✗
Data protection documentation✓ / ✗
AML documentation where applicable✓ / ✗
Board and management records✓ / ✗
Outstanding compliance issues✓ / ✗
Due diligence data room✓ / ✗

The objective is not simply to have every box ticked.

It is to understand where the gaps are before someone external finds them.

The Real Value of Being Review-Ready

Being prepared can provide more than a smoother regulatory review.

It can help the business:

  • Respond faster to information requests
  • Reduce management disruption
  • Identify risks earlier
  • Improve internal organisation
  • Strengthen investor confidence
  • Improve transaction readiness
  • Reduce surprises during negotiations
  • Demonstrate management discipline

In other words:

Regulatory readiness can become a business advantage.

How SHAAS Can Help

At SHAAS, we help businesses assess their readiness before regulatory reviews, investment processes, M&A transactions and other forms of external scrutiny.

Our advisory support can include:

  • Compliance health checks
  • Regulatory readiness assessments
  • Compliance gap analysis
  • Corporate governance reviews
  • Contract and legal document reviews
  • Policy and procedure reviews
  • Internal control assessments
  • Due diligence preparation
  • Data room preparation
  • Compliance remediation
  • Management reporting
  • Ongoing compliance advisory

Our approach is focused on identifying what needs attention, prioritising the risks and helping management address the gaps before they become transaction or regulatory problems.

Don't Wait for the Review to Find the Problem

A regulatory review or due diligence process should not be the first time management asks:

"Are we properly organised?"

The stronger approach is to conduct that assessment before someone else does.

For growing UAE businesses, readiness means being able to demonstrate not only that the company has the right documents, but that it has appropriate processes, controls, accountability and oversight behind those documents.

Would your business be ready if a regulator, investor or buyer requested your records tomorrow?

title: The Importance of Legal Risk Management for UAE Businesses
excerpt: Legal risk rarely starts with a lawsuit. It usually starts much earlier—with a decision, contract, process or obligation that was not properly assessed.
body:
Legal risk rarely starts with a lawsuit. It usually starts much earlier—with a decision, contract, process or obligation that was not properly assessed.

A contract is signed without understanding a liability clause.

A supplier relationship continues despite repeated breaches.

An employee dispute escalates because the company's documentation is weak.

A business enters a new market without assessing its legal requirements.

A regulatory obligation is overlooked.

By the time the issue reaches a lawyer or the courts, the business may already be dealing with financial loss, operational disruption, reputational damage and management distraction.

For UAE businesses, legal risk management is therefore not simply about defending the company when something goes wrong.

It is about identifying legal risks early, assessing their commercial impact and putting appropriate measures in place before those risks become expensive problems.

What Is Legal Risk Management?

Legal risk management is the structured process of:

Identifying → Assessing → Prioritising → Managing → Monitoring

the legal risks that could affect a business.

These risks can arise from:

  • Contracts
  • Employment relationships
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Corporate structure
  • Disputes
  • Intellectual property
  • Data and privacy
  • Suppliers
  • Customers
  • Business expansion
  • Transactions
  • Third parties

The objective is not to eliminate every legal risk.

That is neither realistic nor commercially desirable.

The objective is to ensure that management understands the risks and makes informed decisions about them.

Why Legal Risk Becomes More Important as a Business Grows

Small businesses often rely on relationships and informal arrangements.

The founder may personally know:

  • Every customer
  • Every supplier
  • Every employee
  • Every major contract

As the business grows, this changes.

More employees, customers, suppliers, contracts, jurisdictions and transactions mean more points of legal exposure.

What worked when the company had ten employees may not be sufficient when it has 100.

This is why legal risk management should evolve alongside business growth.

1. Contractual Risk

Contracts are one of the most significant sources of legal and commercial risk.

A poorly drafted or poorly negotiated agreement can expose a business to:

  • Unlimited liability
  • Unclear obligations
  • Unfavourable termination rights
  • Payment disputes
  • Automatic renewals
  • Exclusivity
  • Broad indemnities
  • Intellectual property issues
  • Restrictive covenants
  • Dispute-related costs

The risk is not simply whether the contract is legally valid.

The more important commercial question is:

What happens to the business if the contract does not perform as expected?

Warning Signs

  • Employees sign contracts without legal review.
  • There is no approval process.
  • The business uses templates without understanding them.
  • Material contracts are not centrally tracked.
  • Renewal dates are missed.

2. Regulatory and Compliance Risk

Businesses operate within a regulatory environment that can change as the company grows.

Potential areas include:

  • Licensing
  • Tax
  • Employment
  • AML where applicable
  • Data protection
  • Industry-specific requirements
  • Consumer protection
  • Corporate obligations

A regulatory issue can lead to:

  • Penalties
  • Restrictions
  • Delays
  • Reputational damage
  • Additional regulatory scrutiny

Effective legal risk management therefore requires businesses to understand which legal and regulatory requirements are relevant to their activities.

3. Employment and Workforce Risk

Employees can create significant legal exposure when employment processes are not properly structured.

Potential issues include:

  • Employment contracts
  • Termination
  • Disciplinary action
  • Workplace policies
  • Confidentiality
  • Intellectual property
  • Employee disputes
  • Inconsistent treatment

As the workforce grows, informal management becomes increasingly risky.

Clear documentation and consistent processes can help reduce unnecessary exposure.

4. Corporate Governance Risk

Governance weaknesses can create legal and commercial risks even when the company has not breached a specific regulation.

Examples include:

  • Unclear authority
  • Poor board oversight
  • Conflicts of interest
  • Related-party transactions
  • Founder dependency
  • Weak shareholder arrangements
  • Poor documentation of major decisions

Good governance helps establish:

Who can make decisions.

Who must approve them.

Who is accountable.

How decisions are documented.

5. Dispute Risk

Legal risk management should not begin when a dispute reaches a lawyer's office.

Businesses should identify potential disputes early.

Warning signs can include:

  • Repeated contractual breaches
  • Late payments
  • Customer complaints
  • Supplier disagreements
  • Employee grievances
  • Unresolved correspondence
  • Threats of legal action

Early intervention may provide more options than waiting until the dispute escalates.

6. Intellectual Property Risk

For many businesses, intellectual property is a significant part of enterprise value.

Potential assets include:

  • Trademarks
  • Brand names
  • Copyright
  • Software
  • Designs
  • Business processes
  • Proprietary information
  • Customer databases

Legal risk can arise when ownership is unclear.

For example, a company may pay an external developer to create software but fail to properly address intellectual property ownership in the agreement.

Warning Sign

The business assumes:

"We paid for it, so we own it."

The contractual position should be properly assessed.

7. Confidentiality and Data Risk

Businesses routinely exchange confidential information with:

  • Employees
  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Consultants
  • Investors
  • Potential partners

Without appropriate protections, confidential information can be misused or disclosed.

Legal risk management should therefore consider:

  • NDAs
  • Confidentiality clauses
  • Data protection
  • Access controls
  • Information handling
  • Employee obligations
  • Third-party access

8. Third-Party Risk

Your business can be exposed to legal risk through the actions or failures of third parties.

These may include:

  • Suppliers
  • Agents
  • Distributors
  • Consultants
  • Contractors
  • Outsourced providers
  • Strategic partners

Before entering significant relationships, businesses should consider:

Who are we dealing with?

What obligations are they taking on?

What happens if they fail?

Can we terminate?

Who bears the liability?

What protections do we have?

9. Business Expansion Risk

Expansion often creates new legal questions.

A company entering a new market may need to assess:

  • Corporate structure
  • Licensing
  • Local regulations
  • Employment
  • Tax
  • Contracts
  • Data
  • Intellectual property
  • Distribution arrangements

The mistake is to treat legal review as something that happens after the commercial decision.

Ideally, legal risk should be considered before the business commits significant resources.

10. Transaction Risk

Mergers, acquisitions, investments, joint ventures and strategic partnerships can create substantial legal exposure.

A transaction may require review of:

  • Corporate structure
  • Shareholder rights
  • Contracts
  • Liabilities
  • Litigation
  • Regulatory matters
  • Employment
  • Intellectual property
  • Change-of-control provisions

A legal issue identified late in a transaction can affect:

  • Valuation
  • Negotiations
  • Deal structure
  • Timelines
  • Transaction terms

This is why legal due diligence is an important component of transaction planning.

11. Legal Risk From Poor Documentation

A business may have a reasonable commercial arrangement but weak documentation.

Examples include:

  • Agreements based on emails
  • Verbal commitments
  • Missing amendments
  • Unclear approvals
  • Incomplete records
  • Outdated templates

When relationships are positive, this may not seem important.

When a dispute arises, documentation can become critical.

12. Insurance Does Not Eliminate Legal Risk

Businesses sometimes assume that insurance protects them from all legal exposure.

It does not.

Insurance may address certain financial risks, depending on the policy.

It does not replace:

  • Proper contracts
  • Compliance
  • Governance
  • Internal controls
  • Legal review
  • Risk management

A company should understand both what its insurance covers and what it does not.

13. Legal Risk Should Be Prioritised

Not every legal issue deserves the same level of attention.

A practical risk assessment can consider:

RiskLikelihoodImpactPriority
Major contract liabilityHighHighCritical
Minor contractual issueMediumLowLow
Regulatory breachLowHighHigh
Employee disputeMediumMediumMedium

This helps management focus resources on risks that could materially affect the business.

14. Build a Legal Risk Register

A legal risk register can provide management with visibility over key exposures.

It could include:

  • Risk
  • Business area
  • Likelihood
  • Impact
  • Existing controls
  • Responsible person
  • Mitigation
  • Review date
  • Status

The register should not become another administrative document.

Its purpose is to support better management decisions.

15. Establish Contract Approval Controls

One of the most effective ways to reduce legal risk is to establish a clear contract process.

For example:

Business requirement

↓

Commercial review

↓

Legal review

↓

Risk assessment

↓

Approval

↓

Signature

↓

Contract storage

↓

Ongoing monitoring

This ensures that important agreements do not disappear into individual employees' inboxes.

16. Use Legal Advice Strategically

Not every business decision requires extensive legal advice.

The objective is to involve legal expertise where it adds the most value.

Legal input can be particularly valuable for:

  • Material contracts
  • High-value transactions
  • New markets
  • Regulatory issues
  • Employment disputes
  • Significant customer or supplier disputes
  • Investments
  • M&A
  • Corporate restructuring

The right approach is not:

"Call a lawyer for everything."

It is:

"Know when legal risk could materially affect the business."

Warning Signs Your Business May Have Weak Legal Risk Management

Ask yourself:

  • Do employees sign contracts without legal review?
  • Are important contracts difficult to locate?
  • Are there many verbal agreements?
  • Are contract renewals not systematically tracked?
  • Does the founder personally handle most legal matters?
  • Are policies outdated?
  • Are disputes addressed only after they escalate?
  • Are related-party transactions informal?
  • Is there no legal risk register?
  • Does management know its major legal exposures?
  • Is legal advice sought only after a problem occurs?

Several "yes" answers may indicate that the company would benefit from a structured legal risk review.

Legal Risk Management Is Not About Avoiding Every Risk

Businesses need to take risks to grow.

A company that refuses every contractual, commercial or expansion risk may simply stop growing.

The objective of legal risk management is therefore not:

"Avoid all risk."

It is:

"Understand the risk before making the decision."

This allows management to determine whether the risk should be:

  • Avoided
  • Reduced
  • Transferred
  • Accepted
  • Monitored

That is where legal advice becomes a business decision-making tool, rather than simply a defensive function.

Our legal risk advisory can include:

  • Contract risk reviews
  • Contract management frameworks
  • Regulatory and compliance reviews

  • Transaction support
  • Dispute risk assessment
  • Policies and procedures
  • Legal risk registers
  • Ongoing external legal counsel support

We focus on understanding the commercial impact of legal risk, not simply identifying legal technicalities.

From Legal Problems to Legal Risk Management

The strongest businesses do not wait for a dispute, regulatory issue or failed contract to discover their legal weaknesses.

They identify potential exposure early.

They establish appropriate controls.

They document responsibilities.

They seek advice when it matters.

And they make informed decisions about the risks they are prepared to take.

Legal risk management is ultimately about giving management greater confidence when making important business decisions.

title: 5 Legal Risks Every Growing Company Should Identify
excerpt: Growth is good for business—but growth also changes the company's legal risk profile.
body:
Growth is good for business—but growth also changes the company's legal risk profile.

As a business expands, it typically signs more contracts, hires more employees, works with more suppliers, handles more customer information and makes larger commercial commitments.

What worked when the company was small may no longer provide adequate protection.

The problem is that legal risks often remain invisible until something goes wrong.

A contract dispute can expose weaknesses that existed months earlier. An employee claim can reveal inconsistent HR practices. An investor's due diligence can uncover missing documentation. A new market can create regulatory obligations management had not considered.

For growing UAE businesses, identifying the most important legal risks early can help protect cash flow, reputation, operations and enterprise value.

Here are five areas management should pay particular attention to.

1. Contractual Risk

The contract your business signs today can determine how much risk it carries tomorrow.

As companies grow, the number and value of contracts usually increase.

These may include:

  • Customer agreements
  • Supplier contracts
  • Employment agreements
  • Distribution agreements
  • Partnership arrangements
  • Service agreements
  • Lease agreements
  • Financing arrangements

The risk is not simply having a poorly drafted contract.

It can also arise from accepting commercially unfavourable terms without understanding their consequences.

Common Contract Risks

Look out for:

  • Unlimited liability
  • Broad indemnities
  • Unclear obligations
  • Unfavourable termination rights
  • Automatic renewals
  • Exclusivity provisions
  • Unclear payment terms
  • Excessive warranties
  • Intellectual property ownership issues
  • Restrictive provisions

Warning Signs

Your company may have a contract risk problem if:

  • Employees sign contracts without legal review.
  • Different departments use different templates.
  • Contracts are stored in individual inboxes.
  • Renewal dates are not tracked.
  • There is no contract approval process.
  • Management cannot easily identify its most important contractual obligations.

Why It Matters

A contract may appear acceptable when it is signed but become problematic when:

  • A customer stops paying.
  • A supplier fails.
  • The relationship ends.
  • A project is delayed.
  • A dispute arises.

Good contract management is therefore a risk-management function, not just an administrative task.

2. Employment and Workforce Risk

As the workforce grows, employment decisions become harder to manage informally.

A founder may personally manage employment matters when there are ten employees.

That becomes increasingly difficult with 50, 100 or more employees.

Potential legal risks include:

  • Employment contracts
  • Termination
  • Disciplinary procedures
  • Employee grievances
  • Leave and entitlements
  • Confidentiality
  • Intellectual property
  • Workplace policies
  • Employee data
  • Inconsistent treatment

Warning Signs

Ask:

  • Are all employees working under appropriate documentation?
  • Are HR policies current?
  • Are disciplinary matters handled consistently?
  • Are termination decisions properly documented?
  • Are confidentiality and IP obligations clearly addressed?
  • Does management know who is responsible for HR compliance?

Why It Matters

Employment disputes can consume management time and create financial and reputational consequences.

The greater the workforce, the more important it becomes to have consistent policies, clear procedures and appropriate legal oversight.

3. Regulatory and Compliance Risk

A company can be compliant today and still become exposed tomorrow.

Business activities change.

Companies launch new services, enter new markets, hire more employees, handle more data and develop new commercial relationships.

Each change can potentially affect the company's regulatory obligations.

Depending on the business, areas of concern may include:

  • Licensing
  • Tax
  • Employment
  • AML requirements
  • Data protection
  • Industry-specific regulation
  • Corporate obligations
  • Consumer requirements

Warning Signs

Your compliance framework may need attention if:

  • Nobody has clear responsibility for compliance.
  • Regulatory changes are not monitored.
  • Licences and registrations are tracked manually.
  • Policies have not been reviewed for several years.
  • Compliance issues are discovered only after something goes wrong.

Why It Matters

Regulatory issues can lead to:

  • Penalties
  • Operational disruption
  • Additional scrutiny
  • Reputational damage
  • Delays in expansion

For growing businesses, compliance should therefore be considered before implementing significant commercial changes, rather than afterwards.

4. Corporate Governance and Ownership Risk

Growth can expose weaknesses in how a company is controlled and managed.

Founder-led businesses often operate effectively through personal relationships and informal decision-making.

But as the business grows, questions become more important:

Who can approve major decisions?

Who can sign contracts?

Who controls company funds?

What decisions require shareholder approval?

What happens if shareholders disagree?

What happens if the founder steps away?

Potential risks include:

  • Unclear shareholder rights
  • Weak governance structures
  • Founder dependency
  • Conflicts of interest
  • Related-party transactions
  • Poor board oversight
  • Unclear delegation of authority
  • Weak succession arrangements

Warning Signs

  • Major decisions are made verbally.
  • The founder approves everything.
  • Shareholder arrangements have never been reviewed.
  • There is no formal delegation of authority.
  • Related-party transactions are handled informally.
  • Management responsibilities overlap.

Why It Matters

Governance weaknesses can become particularly visible when a company:

  • Brings in investors
  • Adds new shareholders
  • Expands rapidly
  • Prepares for an acquisition
  • Plans succession
  • Enters due diligence

Good governance creates clarity around ownership, authority and accountability.

5. Legal Risk During Expansion and Transactions

The bigger the business becomes, the more significant its strategic decisions become.

Expansion, investment, joint ventures, acquisitions and major partnerships can introduce substantial legal exposure.

Before entering a significant transaction, businesses should consider:

  • Corporate structure
  • Licensing
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Contracts
  • Shareholder rights
  • Intellectual property
  • Employment
  • Tax
  • Data
  • Existing liabilities
  • Dispute resolution
  • Change-of-control provisions

Warning Signs

Legal risk may not be adequately managed if:

  • Commercial decisions are made before legal implications are assessed.
  • Legal advisers are brought in only after negotiations are substantially complete.
  • No legal due diligence is performed.
  • Existing contracts have not been reviewed before an acquisition.
  • Management does not have a clear view of existing liabilities.

Why It Matters

Legal issues discovered during an investment, acquisition or expansion can affect:

  • Valuation
  • Negotiations
  • Deal structure
  • Transaction timelines
  • Warranties
  • Indemnities
  • Financing

For this reason, legal risk should be considered at the beginning of a strategic transaction—not at the end.

A Simple Legal Risk Test for Growing Companies

Management can start by asking five questions:

QuestionWhat It Reveals
What could go wrong?Potential legal exposure
How likely is it?Risk probability
What would it cost us?Commercial impact
What controls do we have?Existing protection
What should we do next?Risk mitigation

This turns legal risk into something management can actively manage.

Warning Signs Your Business May Need a Legal Risk Review

Consider whether any of the following apply:

  • Contracts are signed without legal review.
  • Important agreements are difficult to locate.
  • The company has no contract register.
  • HR practices are inconsistent.
  • Policies are outdated.
  • The founder manages most legal matters personally.
  • Compliance responsibilities are unclear.
  • Shareholder arrangements have not been reviewed as the company has grown.
  • The company is entering new markets.
  • The company is preparing for investment or a sale.
  • There are unresolved disputes.
  • Management cannot clearly identify its top legal risks.

If several of these apply, it may be time for a structured legal risk assessment.

How SHAAS Can Help

At SHAAS, we help growing businesses identify legal risks before they become costly commercial problems.

Our advisory support can include:

  • Legal risk assessments
  • Contract review and risk management
  • Regulatory and compliance advisory
  • Employment legal advisory
  • Corporate governance
  • Shareholder and corporate structuring
  • Legal due diligence
  • Transaction support
  • Dispute risk assessment
  • External General Counsel support

Our focus is not simply to identify legal issues.

We help management understand what those risks mean commercially, which risks matter most and what practical steps can be taken to manage them.

Growth Should Be Supported by the Right Legal Framework

A growing business should not have to choose between moving quickly and managing legal risk properly.

The objective is to build a legal framework that supports the company's growth.

That means:

Reviewing contracts before they become problems.

Establishing appropriate HR and compliance processes.

Strengthening governance as ownership and management become more complex.

Assessing legal implications before major expansion or transactions.

The earlier these risks are identified, the more options management usually has to address them.

title: How Legal Risk Assessments Protect Businesses Before Problems Occur
excerpt: Most businesses do not discover their legal risks during a legal review. They discover them when something goes wrong.
body:
Most businesses do not discover their legal risks during a legal review. They discover them when something goes wrong.

A customer refuses to pay.
A supplier fails to deliver.
An employee dispute escalates.
A contract creates an unexpected liability.
A regulator asks difficult questions.
An investor identifies a weakness during due diligence.

At that point, management is no longer asking "What could go wrong?"

It is asking:

"How did we let this happen?"

A legal risk assessment is designed to move that conversation earlier.

Rather than waiting for a dispute, regulatory issue or transaction to expose weaknesses, businesses can proactively identify areas of legal exposure, assess their potential impact and decide what action is appropriate.

For growing UAE businesses, this can provide management with greater visibility, stronger decision-making and better protection against avoidable legal problems.

What Is a Legal Risk Assessment?

A legal risk assessment is a structured review of the areas of a business that may create legal exposure.

Depending on the company, this may include:

  • Contracts
  • Corporate structure
  • Governance
  • Employment
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Intellectual property
  • Data protection
  • Customer and supplier relationships
  • Disputes
  • Business expansion
  • Transactions

The purpose is not to find a legal problem in every area.

It is to determine:

What are our material legal risks?

How significant are they?

What controls already exist?

Where are the gaps?

What should management do next?

Why Businesses Often Need a Legal Risk Assessment

Legal risks are not always obvious from day-to-day operations.

A company can be profitable and growing while still carrying significant legal exposure.

For example, it may have:

  • A major customer contract with excessive liability
  • Employment documentation that has not kept pace with the workforce
  • Unclear intellectual property ownership
  • Weak approval processes
  • Outdated policies
  • Unresolved regulatory obligations
  • Poorly documented shareholder arrangements

None of these may create an immediate problem.

But each could become significant when circumstances change.

1. It Identifies Risks Before They Become Disputes

One of the greatest benefits of a legal risk assessment is timing.

Consider a contract that gives a customer broad termination rights.

If identified before signing, the business may be able to negotiate the provision.

If identified after the customer terminates, the options may be significantly more limited.

The earlier a risk is identified, the more opportunities management generally has to address it.

2. It Helps Management Understand Its Exposure

Business owners do not necessarily need to become legal experts.

They need to understand the commercial implications of legal risks.

A useful legal risk assessment should help answer:

  • What is the issue?
  • Why does it matter?
  • How likely is it to occur?
  • What could it cost?
  • What controls exist?
  • What action should be considered?

This allows management to make informed decisions rather than reacting to legal problems after they arise.

3. It Identifies Contractual Weaknesses

Contracts are often one of the first areas reviewed.

A legal risk assessment can consider whether key agreements contain appropriate provisions relating to:

  • Liability
  • Indemnities
  • Termination
  • Payment
  • Confidentiality
  • Intellectual property
  • Exclusivity
  • Warranties
  • Dispute resolution
  • Renewal

The focus should not simply be whether a contract is legally drafted.

It should also be:

Does this contract appropriately protect the company's commercial interests?

4. It Highlights Employment Risks

As companies grow, employment arrangements can become increasingly complex.

A review may identify risks relating to:

  • Employment contracts
  • HR policies
  • Disciplinary processes
  • Termination
  • Confidentiality
  • Intellectual property
  • Employee documentation
  • Inconsistent practices

The goal is not to create unnecessary bureaucracy.

It is to ensure that the company's employment framework is appropriate for its size and workforce.

5. It Identifies Regulatory Gaps

Businesses can face regulatory risk when they:

  • Change activities
  • Launch new services
  • Enter new markets
  • Expand operations
  • Handle additional types of data
  • Become subject to new regulatory requirements

A legal risk assessment can help management identify where its existing compliance framework may need to be strengthened.

This is particularly valuable for companies undergoing significant growth or transformation.

6. It Strengthens Corporate Governance

Governance becomes increasingly important as a company grows.

A legal risk assessment can examine:

  • Decision-making authority
  • Shareholder arrangements
  • Board oversight
  • Delegation of authority
  • Conflicts of interest
  • Related-party transactions
  • Corporate records
  • Founder dependency

The objective is to establish whether the company has appropriate structures around ownership, authority and accountability.

7. It Protects Intellectual Property

Businesses often underestimate the legal importance of their intellectual property.

A legal risk assessment can consider:

  • Who owns the company's IP?
  • Are trademarks properly protected?
  • Are employees' IP obligations documented?
  • Do contractor agreements address ownership?
  • Are confidential business assets adequately protected?
  • Are third-party materials being used appropriately?

These questions become particularly important when the company is preparing for investment or a sale.

8. It Identifies Data and Confidentiality Risks

Companies increasingly depend on information.

A review can consider how the business manages:

  • Customer data
  • Employee information
  • Confidential commercial information
  • Intellectual property
  • Third-party information

It may also consider:

  • NDAs
  • Data protection requirements
  • Access controls
  • Information handling
  • Retention practices

A data-related issue can create both legal and reputational consequences.

9. It Helps Prioritise Legal Risks

Not every legal issue deserves immediate attention.

A good assessment distinguishes between:

High Priority

Potentially significant financial, regulatory or operational consequences.

Medium Priority

Requires action but does not represent an immediate material threat.

Low Priority

Should be monitored or addressed as part of normal business improvement.

This helps management allocate resources where they can have the greatest impact.

10. It Creates a Legal Risk Register

The assessment can be converted into a practical risk register.

For example:

Legal RiskImpactLikelihoodPriorityRecommended Action
Unfavourable customer liability clauseHighMediumHighReview contracts
Outdated HR policiesMediumMediumMediumUpdate framework
Unclear IP ownershipHighLowMediumReview agreements
Missing compliance documentationHighMediumHighRemediation

This turns the assessment into a management action plan, rather than a report that sits in a drawer.

11. It Supports Better Business Decisions

Legal risk should be considered alongside financial and operational considerations.

Before entering a major agreement, management should understand:

What is the commercial opportunity?

What is the financial exposure?

What legal obligations are we accepting?

What happens if the relationship fails?

Can we exit?

Are we comfortable with the risk?

This is where legal risk assessment becomes part of strategic decision-making.

12. It Supports Business Expansion

Expansion creates new legal questions.

Before entering a new market, management may need to consider:

  • Corporate structure
  • Licensing
  • Employment
  • Tax
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Contracts
  • Data protection
  • Intellectual property
  • Local legal requirements

Conducting a legal risk assessment before expansion can help identify issues before capital and resources are committed.

13. It Supports Investment and Due Diligence

Investors and buyers will often examine legal and regulatory risks during due diligence.

Potential areas include:

  • Corporate records
  • Shareholding
  • Contracts
  • Litigation
  • Employment
  • Compliance
  • IP
  • Regulatory matters

A legal risk assessment before due diligence can help management identify issues internally rather than waiting for an investor or buyer to discover them.

This can improve transaction readiness and management confidence.

14. It Can Reduce Management Disruption

Legal problems rarely affect only the legal department.

They can involve:

  • The CEO
  • Finance
  • HR
  • Operations
  • Sales
  • Procurement
  • Board members

A dispute or regulatory problem can consume significant management time.

Identifying risks earlier allows management to address them in a more controlled way.

15. It Supports Stronger Negotiation

Knowledge of legal risk can improve commercial negotiations.

If management knows that a proposed agreement creates significant exposure, it can negotiate from an informed position.

Instead of simply asking:

"Can we sign this?"

the question becomes:

"Which terms create unacceptable exposure, and what protection do we need?"

That is a much stronger commercial approach.

What Does a Legal Risk Assessment Typically Cover?

The scope should depend on the company.

A typical assessment may include:

Corporate

  • Structure
  • Shareholders
  • Governance
  • Authority
  • Corporate records

Commercial

  • Customer contracts
  • Supplier contracts
  • Partnerships
  • Key commercial commitments

Employment

  • Employment documentation
  • Policies
  • Employee processes

Regulatory

  • Licensing
  • Compliance obligations
  • Regulatory exposure

Intellectual Property

  • Trademarks
  • Copyright
  • Software
  • Ownership

Data

  • Privacy
  • Confidentiality
  • Data handling

Disputes

  • Existing disputes
  • Potential claims
  • Contractual conflicts

Strategic

  • Expansion
  • Investment
  • M&A
  • Joint ventures

Warning Signs That Your Business May Need a Legal Risk Assessment

Consider conducting a review if:

  • The business has grown significantly.
  • Contracts have increased substantially.
  • The company has entered new markets.
  • You have hired many new employees.
  • Policies have not been reviewed recently.
  • The founder still handles most legal matters.
  • There is no contract register.
  • There is no legal risk register.
  • You are preparing for investment.
  • You are considering selling the business.
  • You are acquiring another company.
  • You have unresolved disputes.
  • Management cannot identify the company's top legal risks.

What Happens After the Assessment?

The value of an assessment is not the report itself.

The real value is what management does with the findings.

A practical process is:

Identify

↓

Assess

↓

Prioritise

↓

Mitigate

↓

Monitor

↓

Review

Some risks may require immediate action.

Others may simply need monitoring.

Some may be accepted because the commercial opportunity justifies them.

The objective is informed decision-making—not eliminating every risk.

How SHAAS Can Help

At SHAAS, we help businesses proactively identify legal risks and develop practical measures to manage them.

Our legal risk assessment support can include:

  • Contract risk reviews
  • Regulatory and compliance assessments
  • Corporate governance reviews
  • Employment legal risk reviews
  • Intellectual property assessments
  • Data and confidentiality reviews
  • Legal due diligence
  • Dispute risk assessment
  • Legal risk registers
  • Remediation planning
  • Ongoing External General Counsel support

We focus on translating legal risks into clear commercial implications and practical actions for management.

Don't Wait for the Problem to Identify the Risk

A legal dispute, regulatory issue or failed transaction is often the most expensive time to discover a weakness.

A proactive legal risk assessment gives management the opportunity to identify problems while they are still manageable.

For growing UAE businesses, the question should not be:

"Do we have legal risks?"

Every business does.

The more important question is:

"Do we know what our most significant legal risks are—and are we managing them?"

Find out where your business may be exposed before a problem occurs.

title: Contract Risk Management: Protecting Your Business Through Better Agreements
excerpt: A contract can protect your business—or quietly expose it to significant financial and operational risk.
body:
A contract can protect your business—or quietly expose it to significant financial and operational risk.

Many businesses focus on getting a contract signed quickly. The commercial opportunity is urgent, the customer wants to move forward, and management assumes the legal details can be dealt with later.

But once an agreement has been signed, negotiating better protection can become much more difficult.

A poorly structured contract can leave a business exposed to unlimited liability, payment disputes, unclear obligations, difficult termination, unexpected costs and lengthy disputes.

For growing UAE businesses, contract risk management is therefore not simply about reviewing legal wording.

It is about making sure that the agreements supporting the business properly reflect its commercial interests and risk appetite.

What Is Contract Risk Management?

Contract risk management is the process of identifying, assessing and managing the risks associated with a contract throughout its lifecycle.

It begins before the agreement is signed and continues through:

Negotiation → Approval → Signing → Performance → Renewal → Termination

A strong contract risk management approach helps management understand:

  • What obligations the company is accepting
  • What the other party is required to deliver
  • What happens if something goes wrong
  • Where financial exposure exists
  • How the relationship can be terminated
  • Who is responsible for monitoring the agreement

Why Better Agreements Matter

A contract is more than a legal document.

It determines how a commercial relationship operates.

It can define:

  • What will be delivered
  • When payment is due
  • Who bears specific risks
  • What happens when obligations are not met
  • How disputes are handled
  • When the relationship can end

If these issues are unclear, the business may face uncertainty when it matters most.

The objective is not simply to have a legally valid contract. It is to have an agreement that provides appropriate commercial protection.

1. Understand the Commercial Risk Before Reviewing the Contract

A common mistake is to review contracts clause by clause without first understanding the commercial relationship.

Before signing, management should understand:

  • What are we buying or selling?
  • What is the value of the agreement?
  • What are the critical deliverables?
  • What could cause the relationship to fail?
  • What is the potential financial exposure?
  • How important is this customer or supplier?

Without this context, it is difficult to determine whether a contractual provision creates a meaningful business risk.

2. Pay Attention to Liability

Liability provisions can have a disproportionate impact on a company's exposure.

A contract may contain:

  • Liability caps
  • Unlimited liability
  • Exclusions
  • Indemnities
  • Consequential loss provisions
  • Specific damages

Management should understand how these provisions interact.

A contract worth AED 500,000 could potentially create exposure significantly greater than its contract value if liability provisions are not appropriately structured.

Warning Sign

The commercial team knows the contract value but cannot explain the company's maximum potential exposure.

3. Review Indemnities Carefully

Indemnities can transfer significant financial risk from one party to another.

Before accepting an indemnity, businesses should understand:

  • What events trigger it?
  • Is liability limited?
  • Does it cover third-party claims?
  • Is there a financial cap?
  • Is the indemnity reciprocal?
  • Does it overlap with other liability provisions?

A broad indemnity can create obligations that management did not anticipate when negotiating the commercial relationship.

4. Make Obligations Clear

Unclear obligations are a common source of disputes.

Contracts should clearly establish:

  • Scope
  • Deliverables
  • Timelines
  • Responsibilities
  • Performance requirements
  • Acceptance criteria
  • Reporting obligations

If two parties have different interpretations of what was promised, the contract may not provide the certainty management expected.

Warning Sign

Employees regularly need to interpret what a contract means because the scope of work is unclear.

5. Protect Payment and Cash Flow

For many businesses, contractual risk ultimately becomes a cash-flow risk.

Review:

  • Payment terms
  • Invoicing
  • Payment milestones
  • Late payment
  • Disputed invoices
  • Currency
  • Taxes
  • Retention
  • Set-off rights

The contract should provide appropriate protection around one of the most important commercial questions:

When and how does the business get paid?

6. Consider Termination Rights

A contract may work perfectly when the relationship is positive.

The real test comes when the relationship breaks down.

Management should understand:

  • When can either party terminate?
  • Is notice required?
  • Can termination occur for convenience?
  • What happens after termination?
  • What happens to outstanding payments?
  • Are there post-termination obligations?

Unbalanced termination rights can leave a business commercially vulnerable.

7. Manage Contract Renewals

Automatic renewal provisions can create unexpected obligations.

Businesses should monitor:

  • Renewal dates
  • Notice periods
  • Price adjustments
  • Minimum commitments
  • Termination windows

A contract register can help ensure that important dates are not missed.

Warning Sign

The company discovers renewal obligations only after the contractual notice period has expired.

8. Protect Confidential Information

Commercial relationships often involve the exchange of sensitive information.

Contracts should appropriately address:

  • Confidential information
  • Permitted use
  • Disclosure
  • Data handling
  • Return or destruction
  • Survival after termination

For more sensitive transactions, a separate NDA may also be appropriate.

9. Address Intellectual Property

Intellectual property provisions can become particularly important when a business:

  • Develops software
  • Creates content
  • Designs products
  • Uses third-party technology
  • Engages external consultants

The contract should make clear:

Who owns the IP?

Who can use it?

What happens after termination?

Are any licences required?

Assuming ownership without reviewing the contractual position can create problems later.

10. Consider Dispute Resolution

No business enters a contract expecting a dispute.

But management should know what happens if one occurs.

The agreement may address:

  • Governing law
  • Jurisdiction
  • Courts
  • Arbitration
  • Mediation
  • Notice procedures

The dispute resolution mechanism can have significant practical and financial consequences.

11. Manage Third-Party Risk

Supplier and outsourcing contracts can create risks beyond the immediate relationship.

Consider:

  • Subcontracting
  • Data access
  • Confidentiality
  • Service continuity
  • Business interruption
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Insurance
  • Liability

A critical supplier failing can affect your customers even if your own business has done nothing wrong.

12. Avoid One-Sided Agreements

A contract does not necessarily need to be perfectly equal.

Commercial relationships can legitimately allocate more risk to one party.

The important question is:

Is the allocation of risk commercially understood and acceptable?

Management should be particularly careful when:

  • The counterparty has significantly greater negotiating power.
  • The contract is non-negotiable.
  • The business is accepting significant liability.
  • The agreement creates long-term commitments.

13. Establish a Contract Approval Process

Growing companies should avoid allowing anyone to sign any contract without appropriate review.

A practical process could be:

Business request

↓

Commercial review

↓

Risk assessment

↓

Legal review

↓

Management approval

↓

Signature

↓

Contract registration

↓

Ongoing monitoring

The exact process should reflect the size and complexity of the business.

14. Centralise Contract Management

Contracts should not exist only in individual employees' inboxes.

A central contract management system or register should ideally track:

  • Contracting parties
  • Contract value
  • Start date
  • End date
  • Renewal date
  • Notice period
  • Key obligations
  • Responsible person
  • Approval status
  • Important risks

This gives management visibility over its contractual commitments.

15. Monitor Contracts After Signing

Contract risk does not disappear when the agreement is signed.

The company still needs to monitor whether:

  • Obligations are being performed
  • Payments are received
  • Milestones are achieved
  • Notices are issued on time
  • Renewals are managed
  • Breaches are addressed

A strong contract can still create problems if the business fails to manage it properly.

16. Review Contracts Before Major Business Changes

Contracts should be reviewed when the company:

  • Is acquired
  • Receives investment
  • Changes ownership
  • Enters a new market
  • Restructures
  • Changes suppliers
  • Expands operations

Some contracts contain change-of-control or assignment provisions that can become relevant during these events.

Identifying them early can prevent transaction delays.

17. Contract Risk Is More Than Legal Risk

One of the biggest misconceptions is that contract risk belongs exclusively to legal.

It does not.

A contract can create:

Financial Risk

Unexpected costs or lost revenue.

Operational Risk

Inability to deliver or dependence on a third party.

Commercial Risk

Unfavourable pricing or customer obligations.

Regulatory Risk

Non-compliance with applicable requirements.

Reputational Risk

Failure to meet customer or stakeholder expectations.

Effective contract risk management therefore requires commercial, financial, operational and legal perspectives.

A Practical Contract Risk Review

Before signing a significant agreement, management should ask:

QuestionWhy It Matters
What are we committing to?Defines obligations
What does the other party commit to?Defines expectations
What happens if they fail?Determines protection
What happens if we fail?Determines exposure
What is our maximum liability?Measures financial risk
Can we terminate?Determines flexibility
How do we get paid?Protects cash flow
Who owns the IP?Protects enterprise value
How are disputes resolved?Determines enforcement route
Who is responsible for monitoring it?Prevents post-signing failures

The purpose is not to slow down business.

It is to ensure that management understands what it is agreeing to before it commits the company.

Warning Signs Your Business Needs Better Contract Risk Management

You may have a contract risk problem if:

  • Employees regularly sign agreements without legal review.
  • Contracts are stored across different inboxes.
  • There is no central contract register.
  • The business uses templates without reviewing them.
  • Renewal dates are missed.
  • Contracts contain inconsistent terms.
  • Management cannot easily identify major contractual liabilities.
  • Supplier agreements have not been reviewed for years.
  • Customer contracts contain broad liability provisions.
  • There is no clear contract approval authority.

These issues do not necessarily mean that the business is legally exposed.

But they indicate that contract risk may not be sufficiently controlled.

How SHAAS Helps Businesses Manage Contract Risk

At SHAAS, we help businesses manage contractual risk from negotiation through to ongoing contract management.

Our support can include:

  • Contract review
  • Contract risk assessment
  • Contract negotiation support
  • Commercial agreement review
  • Supplier and customer agreement review
  • NDA review
  • Contract management frameworks
  • Contract registers
  • Contract approval processes
  • Contract renewal monitoring
  • Legal due diligence
  • Ongoing External General Counsel support

Our approach combines legal analysis with commercial understanding, helping management understand not only what a clause says, but what it could mean for the business.

Better Contracts Create Better Business Protection

A strong agreement cannot eliminate every commercial risk.

But it can provide clarity around:

Who is responsible.

What must be delivered.

What happens if something goes wrong.

Who bears the risk.

How the relationship can end.

How disputes are handled.

For growing UAE businesses, contract risk management should therefore be treated as part of commercial risk management, not simply a legal formality.
