title: Mergers and Acquisitions Process in the UAE: A Guide for Business Owners
excerpt: Buying or selling a business is one of the most significant decisions a business owner can make. Yet many owners focus heavily on valuation and negotiations while underestimating the legal, regulatory and operational complexity of completing an M&A transaction.
body:
Buying or selling a business is one of the most significant decisions a business owner can make. Yet many owners focus heavily on valuation and negotiations while underestimating the legal, regulatory and operational complexity of completing an M&A transaction.

A successful M&A transaction is not simply:

Agree a price → Sign a contract → Transfer the company.

It typically involves strategy, valuation, structuring, due diligence, negotiation, documentation, regulatory approvals and closing.

For UAE businesses, the process can also vary depending on whether the transaction involves a mainland company, free-zone entity, regulated business, shares, assets or a cross-border structure.

The UAE's legal framework expressly accommodates measures such as ownership transfers, changes of legal form, mergers and acquisitions, while competition rules may also apply to qualifying economic concentrations.

For business owners considering buying, selling or merging a company, understanding the process early can help avoid costly surprises.

What Is an M&A Transaction?

M&A stands for Mergers and Acquisitions.

Although the terms are often used together, they describe different transactions.

Acquisition

One company or investor acquires control of another company or its assets.

Merger

Two businesses combine into a single structure.

Share Acquisition

The buyer acquires shares in the target company and, generally, takes control of the existing corporate entity.

Asset Acquisition

The buyer acquires selected assets or business operations rather than the company's shares.

The appropriate structure depends on the commercial objectives, liabilities, tax considerations, regulatory requirements and circumstances of the transaction.

Why the M&A Process Needs Careful Planning

An M&A transaction can involve multiple parties:

  • Buyer
  • Seller
  • Shareholders
  • Management
  • Lawyers
  • Financial advisers
  • Tax advisers
  • Accountants
  • Valuation advisers
  • Regulators
  • Banks
  • Other stakeholders

Each party has a different role.

A poorly coordinated process can result in:

  • Delays
  • Unexpected liabilities
  • Failed negotiations
  • Regulatory problems
  • Disputes
  • Unfavourable deal terms
  • Value erosion

The earlier the transaction is properly structured, the easier it becomes to manage these risks.

The M&A Process in the UAE

While every transaction is different, a typical M&A process can be divided into the following stages:

1. Strategic Assessment

↓

2. Initial Discussions

↓

3. NDA & Confidentiality

↓

4. Preliminary Terms / Letter of Intent

↓

5. Due Diligence

↓

6. Valuation & Deal Structuring

↓

7. Negotiation & Transaction Documentation

↓

8. Regulatory & Third-Party Approvals

↓

9. Signing

↓

10. Closing & Transfer

↓

11. Post-Transaction Integration

The exact sequence can vary depending on the transaction.

1. Define the Strategic Objective

Before discussing price, the parties should understand why the transaction is taking place.

For a buyer, the objective may be:

  • Entering a new market
  • Acquiring customers
  • Obtaining technology
  • Expanding capacity
  • Acquiring intellectual property
  • Eliminating competition
  • Building scale
  • Diversifying the business

For a seller, the objective may be:

  • Full exit
  • Partial exit
  • Raising capital
  • Finding a strategic partner
  • Succession
  • Unlocking shareholder value

Understanding the objective helps determine the appropriate transaction structure.

2. Identify the Transaction Structure

One of the earliest decisions is whether the transaction should be structured as:

Share Deal

The buyer acquires shares in the target company.

Asset Deal

The buyer acquires selected assets or business operations.

Merger

Two entities combine into a new or existing structure.

Joint Venture

Two or more parties combine resources or ownership for a specific business opportunity.

Each structure has different legal and commercial consequences.

This is why transaction structuring should happen before the parties become committed to a particular deal format.

3. Sign an NDA

M&A discussions usually require the exchange of sensitive information.

This may include:

  • Financial information
  • Customer lists
  • Pricing
  • Contracts
  • Business plans
  • Intellectual property
  • Employee information
  • Strategic information

A properly drafted Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) can establish the rules for handling confidential information.

The NDA should be appropriate to the transaction and should clearly define what information is protected and how it may be used.

4. Preliminary Discussions & Letter of Intent

Once the parties have established interest, they may document the principal commercial terms through a:

  • Letter of Intent
  • Memorandum of Understanding
  • Term Sheet

Depending on the document, it may address:

  • Indicative valuation
  • Transaction structure
  • Proposed consideration
  • Exclusivity
  • Confidentiality
  • Due diligence
  • Conditions
  • Expected timeline

Not every provision needs to be legally binding.

However, business owners should understand which commitments they are actually making before signing.

5. Conduct Legal Due Diligence

This is one of the most important stages of an M&A transaction.

The buyer needs to understand what it is actually acquiring.

Legal due diligence may cover:

Corporate

  • Ownership
  • Shareholding
  • Corporate structure
  • Constitutional documents
  • Board and shareholder records

Commercial Contracts

  • Customer agreements
  • Supplier contracts
  • Distribution agreements
  • Partnerships
  • Material commitments

Employment

  • Employment contracts
  • Key employees
  • Claims
  • Benefits
  • Employee liabilities

Regulatory

  • Licences
  • Approvals
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Industry-specific requirements

Intellectual Property

  • Ownership
  • Registrations
  • Licensing
  • Third-party rights

Litigation

  • Current disputes
  • Potential claims
  • Regulatory investigations

Financing

  • Loans
  • Guarantees
  • Security
  • Shareholder financing

The scope should be tailored to the transaction.

6. Assess the Findings

Due diligence does not automatically mean that every identified issue will stop the transaction.

Instead, the parties need to determine:

What is the risk?

How significant is it?

Can it be corrected?

Who should bear the risk?

Should the transaction price change?

Should additional contractual protection be included?

Potential outcomes can include:

  • Remediation before closing
  • Price adjustment
  • Specific indemnity
  • Warranty protection
  • Escrow or retention
  • Conditions precedent
  • Disclosure

This is where legal due diligence becomes commercially important.

7. Determine the Valuation & Consideration

The purchase price may be based on:

  • EBITDA
  • Revenue
  • Assets
  • Cash flow
  • Comparable transactions
  • Strategic value
  • Future growth
  • Synergies

But the final consideration can also be affected by due diligence findings.

For example, an unexpected liability may affect the price or the structure of consideration.

Payment may involve:

  • Cash
  • Shares
  • Deferred consideration
  • Earn-outs
  • Seller financing
  • A combination of these

8. Negotiate the Transaction

The parties then negotiate the commercial and legal terms.

Key issues may include:

  • Purchase price
  • Payment structure
  • Representations and warranties
  • Indemnities
  • Liability limitations
  • Conditions precedent
  • Completion mechanics
  • Non-compete obligations
  • Confidentiality
  • Post-closing obligations

This is often where the interests of buyer and seller differ significantly.

The seller wants to maximise value and limit continuing liability.

The buyer wants appropriate protection against unknown risks.

9. Consider Regulatory & Competition Requirements

Not every M&A transaction requires the same regulatory approvals.

The applicable requirements depend on factors such as:

  • Industry
  • Transaction structure
  • Size
  • Ownership
  • Jurisdiction
  • Market position
  • Regulatory status

The UAE's competition framework regulates economic concentration, including transactions involving the transfer of ownership or control through mergers and acquisitions. The Ministry of Economy states that qualifying applications are assessed to determine whether the transaction could adversely affect competition.

Regulated sectors can have additional requirements. For example, licensed financial institutions require prior Central Bank approval for certain mergers and acquisitions.

Regulatory analysis should therefore take place early—not after the commercial terms have already been agreed.

10. Signing vs Closing

One of the most important concepts for business owners to understand is that signing and closing are not always the same event.

Signing

The parties execute the transaction documents.

Closing

The conditions required to complete the transaction have been satisfied and the relevant ownership, assets or control are transferred.

There may be a period between signing and closing while parties complete:

  • Regulatory approvals
  • Third-party consents
  • Corporate approvals
  • Financing
  • Documentation
  • Other conditions precedent

The transaction documents should clearly establish what must happen before completion.

11. Complete the Required Corporate & Regulatory Steps

Once the transaction is ready to close, the parties may need to complete the relevant corporate, licensing and registration procedures.

The precise requirements depend on the entity and transaction.

For example, UAE Ministry of Economy procedures for certain foreign-company merger or acquisition registrations require relevant corporate resolutions and evidence of the transaction, with requirements depending on the circumstances.

This is one reason why M&A transactions should not be treated as simply "signing an SPA."

The legal and administrative steps required to give effect to the transaction must also be planned.

12. Post-Transaction Integration

Closing the transaction is not the end.

For an acquisition, management may need to integrate:

  • Employees
  • Systems
  • Finance
  • Contracts
  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Technology
  • Reporting
  • Governance
  • Corporate structures

A transaction can be legally successful but commercially unsuccessful if integration is poorly managed.

This is why buyers should consider post-acquisition integration from the beginning of the process.

What Can Go Wrong During an M&A Transaction?

Business owners should be particularly alert to:

Inadequate Due Diligence

Important liabilities are discovered after closing.

Poor Transaction Structuring

The chosen structure creates unnecessary legal or commercial complications.

Unclear Deal Terms

The parties have different interpretations of what was agreed.

Weak Contractual Protection

The buyer has insufficient protection against identified risks.

Regulatory Delays

Required approvals are not identified early enough.

Incomplete Documentation

Important corporate or commercial records are missing.

Poor Integration Planning

The transaction closes but the expected business benefits are not achieved.

What Should a Buyer Review Before Acquiring a UAE Business?

At a minimum, the buyer should consider reviewing:

  • Corporate structure
  • Share ownership
  • Licences
  • Material contracts
  • Employees
  • Intellectual property
  • Litigation
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Financing
  • Assets
  • Liabilities
  • Tax matters
  • Change-of-control provisions

The scope should be proportionate to the size and complexity of the transaction.

What Should a Seller Do Before Going to Market?

Sellers often focus on making the business attractive to buyers.

They should also make it transaction-ready.

A seller can consider conducting a pre-sale review covering:

  • Corporate records
  • Shareholding
  • Material contracts
  • IP
  • Employment
  • Compliance
  • Litigation
  • Governance
  • Financial and legal liabilities

This allows the seller to identify potential issues before the buyer's advisers do.

It can also make the due diligence process more efficient.

Why Legal Advice Should Start Early

One of the biggest mistakes business owners make is bringing legal advisers into the transaction only when the final agreement is ready to sign.

By then, important commercial decisions may already have been made.

Legal advisers can add greater value when involved early in:

  • Transaction structuring
  • NDA preparation
  • LOI review
  • Due diligence
  • Risk assessment
  • Regulatory analysis
  • Negotiation
  • Transaction documentation
  • Closing

Good legal advice should help shape the transaction—not simply document it.

How SHAAS Supports M&A Transactions

At SHAAS, we support business owners, investors and companies through the legal and strategic aspects of M&A transactions.

Our support can include:

  • M&A Strategy & Transaction Advisory
  • Transaction Structuring
  • Legal Due Diligence
  • Pre-Transaction Legal Health Checks
  • Contract Review
  • Corporate Governance
  • Regulatory & Compliance Review
  • Transaction Documentation
  • Negotiation Support
  • Deal Risk Assessment
  • Closing Support
  • Post-Transaction Advisory

We work to connect legal analysis with commercial objectives, helping clients understand not only what the legal documents say, but what the transaction means for the business.

M&A Is a Business Decision—Not Just a Legal Transaction

Buying or selling a company can fundamentally change the future of a business.

The right transaction can:

  • Accelerate growth
  • Expand market access
  • Create operational synergies
  • Increase enterprise value
  • Provide an exit for shareholders

But poor preparation can create:

  • Unexpected liabilities
  • Disputes
  • Regulatory problems
  • Integration difficulties
  • Loss of value

The strongest transactions are those where strategy, valuation, legal risk and execution are considered together from the beginning.

Whether you are preparing to acquire a company, sell your business or explore a strategic merger, getting the right advice early can make a significant difference.

title: How to Prepare Your Company for Sale
excerpt: Selling a business is not something that should start when you find a buyer. It should start well before you put the company on the market.
body:
Selling a business is not something that should start when you find a buyer. It should start well before you put the company on the market.

A business owner may spend years building revenue, customers, assets and profitability. Yet when the time comes to sell, the transaction can be delayed—or the value of the business reduced—because of issues that could have been addressed months or years earlier.

Unclear ownership.
Weak contracts.
Dependence on the founder.
Incomplete records.
Undocumented intellectual property.
Regulatory gaps.
Unresolved disputes.

These issues can become visible during buyer due diligence and may affect valuation, negotiations, transaction structure and the seller's ability to close the deal on preferred terms.

For UAE business owners considering an exit, preparing the company for sale is therefore about more than finding a buyer.

It is about making the business easier to understand, easier to diligence and easier to acquire.

What Does "Preparing a Company for Sale" Mean?

Preparing a company for sale means reviewing the business before approaching potential buyers to identify and address issues that could affect the transaction.

This may include:

  • Corporate structure
  • Ownership
  • Financial records
  • Commercial contracts
  • Employees
  • Intellectual property
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Litigation
  • Governance
  • Operational dependencies
  • Legal liabilities

The objective is not to make the business look artificially perfect.

It is to ensure that material issues are identified, understood and addressed before the buyer discovers them during due diligence.

Why Should You Prepare Before Finding a Buyer?

Once a buyer is involved, the seller's negotiating position can change.

The buyer's advisers will examine the company and may identify issues that require:

  • Remediation
  • Additional warranties
  • Indemnities
  • Escrow
  • Price reductions
  • Conditions to completion
  • Changes to the transaction structure

If the seller identifies these issues first, there is more time to decide how to deal with them.

The principle is simple:

Prepare privately before negotiating publicly.

1. Clarify Your Ownership Structure

The first question a buyer will want answered is:

Who owns the business?

Review:

  • Shareholding
  • Shareholder agreements
  • Share transfers
  • Corporate records
  • Beneficial ownership
  • Board arrangements
  • Powers and authorities

Any inconsistency between the company's actual ownership and its documentation should be investigated before approaching buyers.

Warning Sign

There are historic shareholder arrangements that were never formally documented or updated.

2. Organise Your Corporate Records

A buyer will likely request corporate documents during due diligence.

These may include:

  • Incorporation documents
  • Constitutional documents
  • Licences
  • Shareholder records
  • Board resolutions
  • Shareholder resolutions
  • Corporate registers
  • Material corporate agreements

If these documents are incomplete or difficult to locate, the transaction can become unnecessarily slow.

A transaction-ready company should have its key corporate records organised before the buyer arrives.

3. Review Your Commercial Contracts

Your contracts represent the commercial relationships that generate the company's revenue and support its operations.

Before selling, review material agreements with:

  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Distributors
  • Partners
  • Franchisees
  • Service providers

Pay particular attention to:

  • Termination rights
  • Change-of-control provisions
  • Assignment
  • Exclusivity
  • Liability
  • Indemnities
  • Renewal
  • Minimum commitments

A buyer may place significant importance on whether key contracts will remain valid after the acquisition.

4. Identify Contracts That Create Risk

Not every contract increases business value.

Some may create significant obligations.

For example:

  • Long-term minimum commitments
  • Unfavourable exclusivity
  • Unlimited liability
  • Significant termination payments
  • Personal guarantees
  • Change-of-control restrictions

A pre-sale legal review can identify these issues before they become negotiation points.

5. Protect Your Intellectual Property

For many companies, intellectual property is a major component of value.

Before a sale, confirm ownership of:

  • Trademarks
  • Software
  • Websites
  • Designs
  • Content
  • Databases
  • Proprietary processes
  • Trade secrets

Particular attention should be given to IP created by:

  • Employees
  • Freelancers
  • Consultants
  • Agencies
  • Technology providers

Warning Sign

The company relies heavily on software, branding or content but cannot clearly demonstrate ownership rights.

6. Review Employment Arrangements

Buyers may want to understand the company's workforce and its employment-related obligations.

Review:

  • Employment contracts
  • Senior management arrangements
  • Key employees
  • Benefits
  • Confidentiality
  • IP provisions
  • Employee disputes
  • Outstanding obligations

Also consider whether the business is overly dependent on the founder or a small number of individuals.

7. Reduce Founder Dependency

A company that cannot operate without its founder can be harder to sell.

Buyers may ask:

  • Who manages the business?
  • Who maintains customer relationships?
  • Who makes key decisions?
  • Who owns the institutional knowledge?
  • What happens when the founder leaves?

A business with established management, documented processes and diversified relationships can often be more attractive to buyers.

The question is:

Are you selling a business—or selling yourself with the business?

8. Review Regulatory & Licensing Matters

Before a sale, confirm that:

  • Licences are current
  • Business activities are properly authorised
  • Required approvals are in place
  • Regulatory obligations are understood
  • Material compliance issues have been identified

This is particularly important where the business operates in a regulated sector or where ownership changes require regulatory approval.

A buyer does not want to discover that the business it is acquiring cannot continue operating under the same structure.

9. Identify Litigation & Potential Claims

Existing litigation should be reviewed before going to market.

But the review should not stop at formal claims.

Consider:

  • Customer disputes
  • Supplier disputes
  • Employee claims
  • Regulatory matters
  • Potential contractual claims
  • Threatened proceedings

The seller should understand the potential financial and commercial impact of these matters and how they may need to be disclosed.

10. Review Debt & Other Liabilities

Buyers will want to understand the company's obligations.

These may include:

  • Bank financing
  • Shareholder loans
  • Guarantees
  • Security
  • Lease commitments
  • Long-term contractual obligations
  • Contingent liabilities

A clear understanding of these obligations can help avoid surprises during negotiations.

11. Strengthen Corporate Governance

A business that is being prepared for sale should ideally have clear governance arrangements.

Review:

  • Board structure
  • Decision-making authority
  • Delegation
  • Shareholder rights
  • Related-party transactions
  • Conflicts of interest
  • Corporate approvals

Weak governance can raise questions about the reliability of the company's decision-making and records.

12. Review Related-Party Transactions

Family-owned and founder-led businesses often have transactions between the company and its owners or related entities.

These may involve:

  • Shared employees
  • Shared premises
  • Loans
  • Management fees
  • Personal expenses
  • Shared assets
  • Related companies

Before a sale, these arrangements should be clearly identified and properly documented.

A buyer needs to understand what actually belongs to the business being acquired.

13. Clean Up the Business Before Due Diligence

The goal is not to hide problems.

It is to identify issues early enough to deal with them properly.

A useful approach is:

Identify

What could concern a buyer?

Assess

How material is each issue?

Remediate

Can the issue be corrected before the sale?

Disclose

Does the buyer need to be informed?

Prepare

How should management respond if the issue becomes part of negotiations?

This gives the seller significantly greater control over the process.

14. Prepare a Due Diligence Data Room

A well-organised data room can significantly improve the transaction process.

It may include:

Corporate

  • Incorporation documents
  • Shareholding
  • Board records
  • Licences

Commercial

  • Customer contracts
  • Supplier agreements
  • Partnerships
  • Major commitments

Employment

  • Key employment agreements
  • HR policies
  • Employee matters

Intellectual Property

  • Registrations
  • Ownership documentation
  • Licensing arrangements

Regulatory

  • Approvals
  • Compliance documentation

Litigation

  • Claims
  • Proceedings
  • Settlement agreements

Financing

  • Loans
  • Guarantees
  • Security documents

The precise scope should be tailored to the business and transaction.

15. Review the Business From a Buyer's Perspective

One of the most valuable exercises before a sale is to ask:

If I were buying this company, what would concern me?

Look at the business objectively.

Would a buyer question:

  • Customer concentration?
  • Founder dependency?
  • Contract quality?
  • Employee retention?
  • IP ownership?
  • Regulatory compliance?
  • Corporate records?
  • Litigation?
  • Unusual liabilities?

Identifying these concerns early allows the seller to prepare a response—or address the underlying issue.

16. Understand What Can Affect Valuation

Legal and operational weaknesses can influence the value a buyer is willing to pay.

For example, a buyer may discount its offer if it discovers:

  • Significant contractual liabilities
  • Weak IP ownership
  • Regulatory uncertainty
  • Major customer concentration
  • Dependence on the founder
  • Unresolved disputes
  • Poor documentation

Preparing the company properly does not guarantee a higher valuation.

But it can reduce avoidable issues that create opportunities for buyers to negotiate the price downward.

17. Decide What Needs to Be Fixed—and What Doesn't

Not every issue needs to be resolved before going to market.

Some issues may be:

  • Immaterial
  • Commercially acceptable
  • Too costly to remediate
  • Better disclosed
  • Appropriate to address through transaction documentation

The key is prioritisation.

A seller should understand the material issues that could affect the transaction and have a strategy for dealing with them.

18. Prepare for Buyer Questions

A serious buyer may ask difficult questions.

The seller should be prepared to explain:

  • Why certain contracts are structured in a particular way
  • How key customers are retained
  • Who owns the IP
  • Why certain related-party transactions exist
  • What litigation exists
  • How the company complies with applicable regulations
  • What happens if the founder leaves

Preparation allows management to answer consistently and confidently.

When Should You Start Preparing Your Company for Sale?

Ideally, 12–24 months before a planned sale if the circumstances allow.

This gives the company time to:

  • Strengthen governance
  • Resolve documentation issues
  • Improve contracts
  • Reduce founder dependency
  • Address regulatory matters
  • Organise records
  • Resolve disputes
  • Build a transaction-ready data room

However, even if the sale is already being considered, it is not too late to conduct a pre-sale review.

Pre-Sale Readiness Checklist

Before approaching buyers, consider whether you can answer "yes" to the following:

Corporate

  • Is ownership clear?
  • Are corporate records complete?
  • Are licences current?

Commercial

  • Are material contracts organised?
  • Have major contractual risks been identified?
  • Are change-of-control provisions understood?

People

  • Are key employment arrangements documented?
  • Is the business overly dependent on the founder?

IP

  • Does the company clearly own its key intellectual property?

Compliance

  • Are regulatory obligations understood and addressed?

Risk

  • Are litigation and potential claims identified?
  • Are debt and other liabilities clearly documented?

Transaction

  • Is the company ready for legal due diligence?
  • Can requested documents be provided quickly?
  • Has management identified likely buyer concerns?

If several answers are "no" or "I'm not sure," the company may benefit from a structured pre-sale readiness review.

How SHAAS Helps Prepare Companies for Sale

At SHAAS, we help business owners prepare their companies for a potential sale by identifying legal and commercial issues before they become transaction obstacles.

Our support can include:

  • Pre-Sale Legal Readiness Reviews
  • Legal Health Checks
  • Legal Due Diligence Preparation
  • Corporate Governance Review
  • Commercial Contract Review
  • Legal Risk Assessment
  • Regulatory & Compliance Review
  • Intellectual Property Review
  • Employment Documentation Review
  • Data Room Preparation
  • M&A & Transaction Advisory
  • Negotiation Support

Our objective is to help owners enter the sale process prepared, informed and in control of their legal position.

Don't Wait for the Buyer to Find the Problems

A buyer's due diligence is designed to identify risk.

A seller's preparation should do the same—but before the buyer does.

The earlier you identify weaknesses, the more options you have to address them.

You can fix them, disclose them, negotiate them or prepare appropriate contractual protection.

What you do not want is to discover a material issue for the first time after you have already committed to selling your business.

Thinking about selling your company?

Start preparing before you approach the market.

title: Key Legal Risks Buyers Should Consider Before Acquiring a Business
excerpt: Buying a business is not simply about deciding whether the numbers look attractive.
body:
Buying a business is not simply about deciding whether the numbers look attractive.

A company can have strong revenue, healthy margins and an impressive customer base—and still carry legal risks that could materially affect its value after acquisition.

A buyer may discover after signing or completing a transaction that:

  • A key contract can be terminated after a change of ownership.
  • Intellectual property is not actually owned by the target.
  • Important employees have weak contractual arrangements.
  • Regulatory approvals are incomplete.
  • A major dispute was not properly disclosed.
  • The company's corporate records are inconsistent.
  • Significant liabilities were hidden within contractual arrangements.

These issues can create financial exposure, operational disruption, disputes and unexpected costs.

For buyers considering an acquisition in the UAE, legal due diligence should therefore be viewed as an important part of investment and risk assessment—not simply a legal formality.

Why Legal Risk Matters When Acquiring a Business

When you acquire a company, you may also acquire its:

  • Contracts
  • Employees
  • Obligations
  • Intellectual property
  • Regulatory exposure
  • Existing disputes
  • Historical liabilities

The buyer therefore needs to understand not only what the business owns, but also what it is legally committed to.

A strong financial performance does not automatically mean that the business has a strong legal position.

1. Ownership & Corporate Structure Risk

The first question should be:

Does the seller actually have the right to sell what you are buying?

The buyer should understand:

  • Share ownership
  • Shareholder arrangements
  • Beneficial ownership
  • Corporate structure
  • Share transfers
  • Existing shareholder rights
  • Board arrangements
  • Corporate approvals

Any uncertainty around ownership can create serious transaction risk.

Warning Sign

The company's corporate documents do not clearly reflect its current ownership or historical changes in shareholding.

2. Contractual Risk

A company's contracts are often central to its value.

A buyer should review material agreements with:

  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Distributors
  • Partners
  • Franchisees
  • Service providers

Particular attention should be given to:

  • Termination rights
  • Change-of-control provisions
  • Assignment
  • Exclusivity
  • Minimum commitments
  • Liability
  • Indemnities
  • Renewal

A business may appear highly profitable until the buyer discovers that its most important customer can terminate the contract following an acquisition.

The question is not simply:

"Does the company have contracts?"

It is:

"What happens to those contracts after we acquire the company?"

3. Intellectual Property Risk

For technology, professional services, creative and consumer businesses, IP can represent a substantial portion of enterprise value.

The buyer should establish:

  • What IP exists
  • Who owns it
  • Whether ownership is documented
  • Whether it is registered
  • Whether third parties have rights
  • Whether employees or contractors created it

This is particularly important for:

  • Software
  • Trademarks
  • Websites
  • Databases
  • Designs
  • Content
  • Proprietary processes

Warning Sign

The seller claims ownership of important IP but cannot provide clear documentation establishing ownership.

4. Regulatory & Licensing Risk

A buyer needs confidence that the target can legally continue operating after the acquisition.

Review:

  • Trade licences
  • Business activities
  • Regulatory approvals
  • Industry-specific requirements
  • Compliance obligations
  • Regulatory correspondence

This becomes particularly important in regulated industries.

The buyer should also understand whether the change in ownership itself triggers approvals, notifications or other regulatory requirements.

5. Litigation & Dispute Risk

Existing disputes can significantly affect an acquisition.

Review:

  • Court proceedings
  • Arbitration
  • Customer disputes
  • Supplier claims
  • Employment claims
  • Regulatory investigations
  • Potential claims

The important question is not only:

"Is the company currently being sued?"

It is also:

"Are there circumstances that could reasonably develop into a claim?"

6. Employment & Workforce Risk

Employees can represent both value and liability.

A buyer should consider:

  • Employment contracts
  • Key management
  • Employee benefits
  • Termination obligations
  • Confidentiality
  • IP ownership
  • Employee disputes
  • Outstanding liabilities

Particular attention should be paid to key employees whose departure could materially affect the business.

7. Founder Dependency Risk

This is particularly important when acquiring SMEs and founder-led businesses.

If the founder personally controls:

  • Customer relationships
  • Supplier relationships
  • Business development
  • Key decisions
  • Operational knowledge
  • Strategic relationships

then the buyer may not actually be acquiring a self-sustaining business.

Warning Sign

A significant percentage of revenue depends on relationships that exist primarily because of the seller personally.

The transaction may therefore require:

  • A transition period
  • Retention arrangements
  • Consulting agreements
  • Non-compete provisions
  • Management succession

8. Debt & Financial Obligation Risk

A buyer should understand the company's existing obligations.

These may include:

  • Bank loans
  • Shareholder loans
  • Guarantees
  • Security arrangements
  • Leases
  • Long-term commitments
  • Deferred obligations
  • Contingent liabilities

In a share acquisition, understanding the company's existing liabilities is particularly important because the legal entity generally continues to exist after the transaction.

9. Tax & Statutory Compliance Risk

Legal due diligence should be coordinated with appropriate financial and tax due diligence.

The buyer may need to understand:

  • Tax registrations
  • Filing history
  • Outstanding obligations
  • Tax disputes
  • Penalties
  • Statutory compliance

In the UAE, this may include relevant VAT and Corporate Tax considerations, depending on the target and transaction structure.

Tax analysis should be undertaken by appropriately qualified tax advisers alongside the legal due diligence process.

10. Related-Party Transaction Risk

Founder-led businesses frequently have arrangements with related parties.

These might include:

  • Shareholder loans
  • Management fees
  • Shared employees
  • Shared premises
  • Related companies
  • Personal expenses
  • Shared assets

The buyer needs to understand whether these arrangements will:

  • Continue after acquisition
  • Be terminated
  • Require restructuring

A business may look more profitable or less profitable than it actually is depending on how related-party arrangements are treated.

11. Data Protection & Confidentiality Risk

Businesses increasingly hold substantial amounts of information.

This may include:

  • Customer data
  • Employee information
  • Commercial information
  • Financial records
  • Proprietary data

The buyer should understand how the target handles and protects sensitive information and whether relevant contractual and regulatory obligations have been addressed.

Data-related issues can become particularly important in technology, healthcare, financial services and other data-intensive businesses.

12. Compliance & Internal Policy Risk

The buyer should assess whether the target has appropriate policies and procedures for its size and activities.

Depending on the business, this could include:

  • Compliance policies
  • Anti-bribery procedures
  • Conflict-of-interest controls
  • Data protection policies
  • HR policies
  • Delegation of authority
  • Internal approval procedures

A company does not necessarily need a complex compliance framework.

It needs one that is appropriate to its risk profile.

13. Change-of-Control Risk

This deserves particular attention.

Some contracts may provide that a change in ownership:

  • Requires consent
  • Triggers termination
  • Allows renegotiation
  • Requires notification

Imagine acquiring a company where its largest customer represents 40% of revenue—and the customer has the right to terminate if ownership changes.

That contractual provision could materially affect the value of the acquisition.

Change-of-control clauses should therefore be identified early.

14. Asset Ownership Risk

The buyer should verify that the assets presented as part of the business actually belong to the target.

This may include:

  • Equipment
  • Vehicles
  • Property
  • Software
  • Intellectual property
  • Inventory
  • Databases

Questions should include:

Who owns the asset?

Is it leased or financed?

Is there any security over it?

Can it be transferred?

15. Real Estate & Lease Risk

Where the business depends on physical premises, the buyer should review:

  • Lease agreements
  • Term
  • Renewal
  • Rent obligations
  • Termination
  • Assignment
  • Change-of-control provisions
  • Security deposits

A business may depend heavily on a particular location, making the lease commercially critical.

16. Hidden or Contingent Liabilities

Not every liability appears clearly on the balance sheet.

Potential exposure may arise from:

  • Guarantees
  • Indemnities
  • Pending claims
  • Contractual commitments
  • Regulatory matters
  • Employee claims
  • Long-term obligations

This is why legal and financial due diligence need to work together.

17. Corporate Governance Risk

A buyer should understand how the company has historically been managed.

Review:

  • Board approvals
  • Shareholder resolutions
  • Delegation
  • Related-party transactions
  • Conflicts of interest
  • Corporate records

Poor governance can create uncertainty around whether decisions were properly authorised and documented.

18. Data Room & Documentation Risk

The quality of the target's documentation can itself provide useful information.

If the seller cannot readily provide:

  • Contracts
  • Corporate documents
  • Licences
  • IP records
  • Employment documentation
  • Litigation records

it may indicate weaknesses that require further investigation.

A disorganised data room does not automatically mean a bad business—but it is a reason to ask more questions.

What Should Buyers Do When They Identify a Legal Risk?

Finding a legal risk does not automatically mean:

"Walk away from the deal."

Instead, the buyer should assess:

1. Materiality

How significant is the risk?

2. Probability

How likely is it to cause a problem?

3. Financial Impact

What could it cost?

4. Remediation

Can it be fixed before closing?

5. Allocation

Who should bear the risk?

6. Protection

Can the buyer obtain contractual protection?

Possible solutions may include:

  • Price adjustment
  • Warranty
  • Indemnity
  • Escrow
  • Retention
  • Condition precedent
  • Remediation before closing
  • Specific contractual undertaking

Legal Due Diligence Should Support the Deal—Not Just Identify Problems

A good legal due diligence process should answer three questions:

What are we buying?

Understanding the legal assets and rights being acquired.

What are we inheriting?

Identifying liabilities, obligations and potential exposure.

What should we do about it?

Translating findings into transaction decisions.

This is where legal due diligence becomes commercially valuable.

Red Flags Buyers Should Not Ignore

Consider slowing down and investigating further if:

  • Ownership is unclear.
  • Material contracts are missing.
  • Key customer agreements contain change-of-control restrictions.
  • IP ownership cannot be demonstrated.
  • Significant disputes exist.
  • Regulatory approvals are unclear.
  • Corporate records are incomplete.
  • Major liabilities are poorly documented.
  • The business depends heavily on the founder.
  • Related-party transactions are extensive.
  • The seller is reluctant to provide information.

None of these automatically means the acquisition should stop.

But each warrants proper investigation and commercial assessment.

When Should Legal Due Diligence Start?

Ideally, legal due diligence should begin before the buyer becomes irrevocably committed to the transaction.

The earlier significant risks are identified, the more options the buyer has to:

  • Renegotiate
  • Restructure
  • Seek protection
  • Require remediation
  • Adjust valuation
  • Walk away

Discovering a major issue after signing a binding agreement may leave the buyer with significantly fewer options.

How SHAAS Supports Buyers

At SHAAS, we help investors and business owners assess legal risks before acquiring a company.

Our support can include:

  • Legal Due Diligence
  • M&A Advisory
  • Transaction Risk Assessment
  • Corporate Structure Review
  • Contract Review
  • IP Review
  • Regulatory & Compliance Review
  • Employment & HR Legal Review
  • Litigation Review
  • Corporate Governance Review
  • Transaction Structuring
  • Negotiation Support
  • Closing Support

Our approach is focused on helping buyers understand what the legal risks mean commercially, not simply producing a long list of legal findings.

Don't Buy the Business Before Understanding the Risk

A successful acquisition is not simply about buying a profitable company.

It is about understanding what sits behind the profitability.

Strong revenue can be undermined by a weak contract.

Valuable technology can be undermined by unclear IP ownership.

A strong customer base can be undermined by change-of-control provisions.

An attractive business can be undermined by unresolved liabilities.

Before you acquire a business, know what you are actually acquiring.

If you are considering an acquisition in the UAE, SHAAS can help you assess the legal risks before they become your risks.
